clue.text: What you get when you spill your glass while sitting things out? (It may have to be treated.)

definitions.text: What you get when you spill your glass while sitting things out? (It may have to be treated.)

parts.words: spill your glass while sitting things out
parts.note: read literally, a drink knocked over onto your lap while you sit out a dance soaks the joint in your leg

parts.words: It may have to be treated
parts.note: the bracket switches to the medical sense: fluid on a joint is a condition a doctor treats

explanation.surface: A wallflower sitting out the dances knocks a drink over and wonders what to call the result.
explanation.walkthrough: WATER ON THE KNEE is both a literal description of a spilt drink on a seated lap and the everyday name for fluid swelling the knee joint.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the common name for an effusion of fluid in the knee joint, a complaint needing medical treatment.

clue.text: With such as clarinets and saxophones, you shouldn't have to, as you must with old turntables.

definitions.text: With such as clarinets and saxophones, you shouldn't have to, as you must with old turntables.

parts.note: clarinets and saxophones are blown, so they belong to the woodwind family of the orchestra

parts.words: you shouldn't have to, as you must with old turntables
parts.note: read as a verb phrase: wind-up gramophones had to be cranked by hand, unlike a clarinet, which needs no winding

explanation.surface: A musician compares modern woodwinds with the old hand-cranked record players.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is read twice: as a noun for blown instruments, and as an instruction to crank up a machine, which old gramophones needed and clarinets do not.
explanation.definitionFit: Clarinets and saxophones are classed as wind instruments because the player's breath makes the sound.

clue.text: Its diet is certainly different, though least messy.

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase are rearranged into something quite different, so the words are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pet food advert boasts that this animal's diet is unlike any other and the least messy.
explanation.definitionFit: Tidiest is the superlative of tidy, the opposite of messy, so it means the least untidy.

clue.text: One with a forked tongue is coming up here, when traveling by it.

definitions.note: the answer completes the phrase traveling by ___, a mode of transport rather than a noun on its own

indicators.note: in a down clue, something coming up here is read from the bottom of the light upwards, so it is reversed

parts.note: to speak with forked tongue is to lie, so this is a liar

explanation.surface: A traveller warns that a snake is coming up the path here.
explanation.walkthrough: The forked tongue suggests a snake, but it is the idiom for lying. The definition is the phrase traveling by rail with the answer left out.
explanation.definitionFit: Traveling by rail means going by train, the railway being the means of transport.

clue.text: Grading letters from a very stingy person.

indicators.note: the answer is made of the letters taken from the word and put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A teacher's grading notes go out from a notoriously mean colleague.
explanation.definitionFit: A niggard is an old word for a miser, someone who spends or gives as little as possible.

clue.text: A foot soldier of old Greece gets a head start, and could be polite finally.

definitions.text: A foot soldier of old Greece

indicators.note: the rearranged word comes at the end, after the opening letter
the start of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: only its first letter is used

indicators.note: the word is something the letters could become when rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek infantryman gets ahead of the field, and might at last be courteous.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoplites were the heavily armed citizen infantry of the ancient Greek city-states.

clue.text: See 1
In Paris no sort of post could be expected to go on indefinitely.

definitions.text: could be expected to go on indefinitely
definitions.note: describes something rather than naming it, matching the adjective

parts.note: non is the French word for no

indicators.note: a sort of post is the word rearranged into something like it

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: In Paris, some kind of posting looks set to last forever.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nonstop continues without a break, so it seems to go on without end.

clue.text: A classic example of tightness.

parts.note: the example comes from a classic, Dickens's A Christmas Carol
tight is slang for mean with money, not physically taut

explanation.surface: A textbook case of something being pulled taut.
explanation.walkthrough: Tightness looks physical, like a knot or a muscle, but tight here means miserly.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebenezer Scrooge, the miser of Dickens's A Christmas Carol, is the proverbial skinflint.

clue.text: Gets in, having no romantic companion, but flooded by the response.

parts.note: taken as written
someone without a date is, jokingly, undated

explanation.surface: Someone gets into a party alone but is then swamped by the reaction.
explanation.definitionFit: To be inundated with replies is to be overwhelmed, as if by a flood of water.

clue.text: Describing the acquaintance you barely know, but who appears to be a bit tired?

definitions.text: Describing the acquaintance you barely know
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a ... acquaintance is someone you know only well enough to nod to

definitions.text: who appears to be a bit tired
definitions.meaning: second meaning: dozing off, head dropping with sleepiness

explanation.surface: A casual acquaintance seems a little worn out when you meet.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective fits the idiom nodding acquaintance and also describes someone drowsily drooping their head.

clue.text: If you do it, you may be sorry!

definitions.text: If you do it, you may be sorry!

parts.note: the answer is something one does, as in the phrase do ___
sounds like a warning of regret to come, but means the doer is already contrite

explanation.surface: A warning that some action will lead to regret.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation reads as a threat of later regret; in fact being sorry is why one performs this act.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing penance is an act of self-punishment or devotion performed to show repentance for a wrong.

clue.text: Something on the list which may be a mite different.

indicators.note: the letters are made different by being reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: One entry on a list is just a little bit unusual.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is a single entry or thing in a list or collection.

clue.text: An unimposing figure of a man, but namely a governor of New York with something to catch, and returning to a Parisian.

definitions.text: An unimposing figure of a man

parts.words: namely a governor of New York
parts.note: Mario Cuomo was governor of New York; namely means by his first name
a net is used to catch fish or butterflies

indicators.note: the word is turned back to front

parts.note: et is French for and, the language signalled by to a Parisian

explanation.surface: A slight figure of a man turns out to be a New York governor with something to catch, heading back to France.
explanation.walkthrough: Mario Cuomo was Governor of New York from 1983 to 1994. The French for and is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A marionette is a puppet worked by strings, a small figure of a person with no will of its own.

clue.text: A group of players is about finished, and left out cold!

indicators.note: the group surrounds the other word, so it goes around it

parts.note: a band is a group of musicians
something done is finished

explanation.surface: A sports team has nearly finished and is left outdoors in the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: Players looks like a sports team, but they are musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: To be left out in the cold is to be deserted, ignored or forsaken.

clue.text: You shouldn't expect to have one follow your behavior if you do.

definitions.text: You shouldn't expect to have one follow your behavior if you do.

parts.words: You shouldn't expect to have one follow
parts.note: the one followed is the model you provide, which nobody should copy
the answer describes behaving badly in front of others

explanation.surface: A parent's warning: behave like that and don't expect anyone to copy you.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that an example is meant to be followed, but this kind should not be.
explanation.definitionFit: To set a bad example is to behave in a way others should not imitate.

clue.text: See 15
Proving the communists are about to come first, as one does to watch every day if you have the right kind of a ticker.

definitions.text: as one does to watch every day if you have the right kind of a ticker
definitions.note: describes what one does, matching the third-person verb

indicators.note: the communists go around the other word

parts.note: Reds is the old nickname for communists
to win is to finish first

explanation.surface: Evidence that the communists are about to win, mixed up with the daily habit of a watch owner.
explanation.walkthrough: A ticker is slang for a watch, and also for the heart, which is the misdirection. A mechanical watch must be wound up again each day.
explanation.definitionFit: One rewinds a mechanical watch daily to keep its spring tensioned and the watch running.

clue.text: Lived at one time to go over the water–"Here's to your health!"

definitions.note: a toast, which the answer is as an old exclamation

parts.note: was is the past tense of be, so it means existed once
to sail is to cross the water in a boat

explanation.surface: An old sailor toasts a voyage over the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Wassail comes from Old English for be in good health, a toast drunk at festivities.

clue.text: Part of the fugue could be a sort, and in Paris it comes to a junction inside it.

indicators.note: the pieces go inside the rearranged word
the word is something its letters could become when rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
et is French for and
a T-junction, so T

explanation.surface: A musician says part of a fugue might be one sort, while in Paris it reaches a junction.
explanation.walkthrough: A T-junction is where one road meets another at right angles.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretto is the passage in a fugue where entries of the subject overlap, coming close together.

clue.text: A bit confused, Lear suffers a setback by the father of Odysseus.

indicators.note: the name is lightly mixed up, its letters rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
read as two words, set back: the word set written backwards

explanation.surface: A muddled King Lear suffers a blow beside the father of Odysseus.
explanation.walkthrough: Setback looks like a misfortune, but split it into set and back.
explanation.definitionFit: Laertes, king of Ithaca, was the father of Odysseus in Homer's Odyssey.

clue.text: With a heavy weight away from it, it's at least a start!

parts.note: lead is a proverbially heavy metal
off means away

explanation.surface: With a heavy load removed, at least a beginning has been made.
explanation.walkthrough: A weight off your mind is the false picture; the pieces are the metal and off.
explanation.definitionFit: A leadoff is the opening move or first item, the one that begins proceedings.

clue.text: The sort found sort of near a city.

indicators.note: to sort letters is to put them in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the word rearranged into something like it

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The kind of person found living close to a city.
explanation.walkthrough: TEHERAN is an older spelling of Tehran, the capital of Iran.
explanation.definitionFit: Tehran, also spelt Teheran, is the capital city of Iran.

clue.text: If one insists "Show me!" he or she may be one.

definitions.text: If one insists "Show me!" he or she may be one.

parts.note: Missouri's nickname is the Show-Me State, for its people's supposed demand for proof

parts.words: he or she may be one
parts.note: the answer is a person from that state

explanation.surface: A sceptic who demands proof is probably a certain type of person.
explanation.walkthrough: Missouri, a US state, is nicknamed the Show-Me State, after its residents' reputation for being hard to convince.
explanation.definitionFit: A Missourian is a native of Missouri, the state proverbially insisting on evidence before believing.

clue.text: If she's a Londoner, she could certainly keep busy around the house, and slightly burn the fish!

definitions.text: If she's a Londoner, she could certainly keep busy around the house
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a ..., short for charwoman, is a cleaning lady
second meaning: to scorch the surface
third meaning: a fish of the trout family

explanation.surface: A busy London housewife scorches the fish she is cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: Char, or charwoman, is British for a woman paid to clean houses.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a cleaning woman, to scorch lightly, and a cold-water fish related to trout.

clue.text: What may go in the collar of a horse is a kind of poker.

definitions.text: What may go in the collar
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a collar ... fastens a detachable shirt collar
second meaning: a stallion kept for breeding
third meaning: ... poker, where some cards are dealt face up

explanation.surface: Something tucked into a horse's collar turns out to be a sort of poker.
explanation.walkthrough: The collar of a horse is the false picture; the collar is a shirt's and the horse is separate.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a collar fastener, a breeding stallion, and a poker variant with face-up cards.

clue.text: In earnest, but slightly confused, you have the closest thing to it.

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the superlative adjective

indicators.note: the word's letters are a little mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone in earnest but a bit muddled has nearly got there.
explanation.definitionFit: Nearest is the superlative of near, so it means closest in distance or likeness.

clue.text: Not a slight change when going to a place in South America, as they say–but this is in Canada.

definitions.note: a place described rather than named, standing for the province

indicators.note: the answer is what the phrase sounds like when spoken

parts.words: going to a place in South America
parts.note: heading on to Rio de Janeiro, so on to Rio

explanation.surface: Moving on to somewhere in South America is a big change, though this place is in Canada.
explanation.walkthrough: Not a slight change is the setter's joke about the distance; on to Rio said quickly sounds like the province's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ontario is the most populous province of Canada, home to Toronto and Ottawa.

clue.text: Having this, you can't be afraid to do most jobs!

definitions.text: Having this, you can't be afraid to do most jobs!

parts.note: the answer is a quality a person possesses

parts.words: you can't be afraid to do most jobs
parts.note: describes the assurance to take on any task without fear

explanation.surface: A career adviser's pep talk about the quality that lets you tackle anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-confidence is trust in one's own abilities, which stops someone fearing a task.
